title: CBSE Dumps the Vendor Behind Its Exam Scandal. IIT Has Built a Replacement.
excerpt: Coempt EduTeck's portal had expired security certificates, multiple data access vulnerabilities, and was hit by a 3.8-million-packet cyberattack. The new IIT-audited system is now live.
body:
The Central Board of Secondary Education has formally severed ties with the private vendor at the centre of India's biggest exam technology scandal. CBSE will no longer use the Coempt EduTeck platform for its re-evaluation process, and an IIT panel has now given full security clearance to a new examiner-facing portal built with assistance from IIT Kanpur, IIT Madras, and the Digital India Corporation.

The move, confirmed on June 8, closes a turbulent chapter that began when whistleblowers flagged serious vulnerabilities in Coempt EduTeck's On-Screen Marking system — the digital infrastructure through which approximately 40 crore pages of Class 12 answer sheets were scanned and evaluated.

"There were many security weaknesses in that portal, which allowed access to data and records," an IIT panel member told ANI. "There are multiple ways through which data could be accessed. We had to go through carefully, close all the possibilities."

What IIT Found

The security audit uncovered a pattern of negligence that extended beyond code vulnerabilities. According to reports, the cybersecurity certificates that Coempt EduTeck submitted to CBSE were issued for a different client's deployment of the same software, tested in a pre-production staging environment. In one case, the certificate was nearly two years old when submitted — its own validity clause states it lapses after one year or when the application is modified.

The new portal retains the core functionality of the Coempt system but has been rebuilt with what the IIT panel describes as "significant changes in terms of security, not functionality." All examination-related data and records have been migrated from vendor-controlled servers to infrastructure managed directly by CBSE.

The Cyberattack That Followed

The security overhaul came under immediate real-world pressure. On June 3, one day after CBSE's post-result services portal went live, attackers launched a coordinated Denial-of-Service strike involving approximately 3.8 million malicious data packets. Within minutes of the portal becoming operational, security systems also detected and blocked over 100,000 unauthorised access attempts.

CBSE said the attacks were mitigated successfully and no student data was compromised. Delhi Police has filed an FIR and launched an investigation. Cybersecurity teams from IIT Kanpur, IIT Madras, CERT-In, and the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) assisted in handling the assault.

Despite the attacks, the portal processed over 70,433 applications by June 4 — including 7,314 for verification of marks and 63,119 for re-evaluation. The application window closed on June 7 after a one-day extension granted because of technical difficulties caused by the traffic surge.

Why This Matters Beyond the Exam Hall

The CBSE OSM scandal is no longer a story about one year's board results. It has become a stress test for India's capacity to digitise high-stakes public infrastructure without outsourcing accountability to private vendors whose security practices go unaudited.

The 18-year-old ethical hacker from Ranchi who first exposed the OSM vulnerabilities, the 400,000 students who applied for rechecks, the IIT Roorkee admission crisis that followed — each of these ripples originated from the same root failure: a government board that trusted a vendor with the integrity of 40 crore answer sheets without independently verifying the vendor's security posture.

For NRI families with children applying to IITs, NITs, and top universities through CBSE scores, the implications are direct. A compromised grading system means compromised admissions. The IIT-backed portal is a corrective step, but trust, once broken at this scale, takes more than a security patch to restore.

The re-evaluation results, once processed through the new portal, will be treated as final. Revised marks will be reflected in updated marksheets. For tens of thousands of students whose futures hinge on the difference between a few marks, the hope is that this time, the technology behind the grade is as rigorous as the exam itself.

Sources: ANI, Livemint, Dainik Bhaskar, NewKerala, DevDiscourse
